solution: 1) speed, stack of limits, cntNo = 0, ans = 0. 2) Type 1: speed = s; pop (ans++) while top < speed. 3) Type 3: push s; pop (ans++) while top < speed. 4) Type 5: clear stack. 5) Type 2 (overtake): ans += cntNo, cntNo = 0. 6) Type 4: cntNo = 0. Type 6: cntNo++.
dry_run: Sample: speed 100; sign 70 -> ignored (ans 1); overtake ok; 120 pushed, no-limit clears; 120 pushed; no-overtake cnt=1; speed 150 pops 120 (ans 2); overtake-allowed resets cnt; 300 pushed. Answer 2.

brief: n students in a row; string of L/R/= for each adjacent pair says who has higher marks. Give each at least 1 toffee, higher marks -> more toffees than neighbor, equal -> equal; minimize total.
key_idea: Start everyone at 1 and repeatedly raise values to satisfy each constraint (least fixpoint); this gives the minimum.
solution: 1) c[i]=1. 2) Repeat until no change: for each i: 'R' -> c[i+1] = max(c[i+1], c[i]+1); 'L' -> c[i] = max(c[i], c[i+1]+1); '=' -> both = max(c[i], c[i+1]). 3) Print c. (n<=1000 so repeated sweeps are fast; alternately left and right sweeps converge quickly.)
dry_run: Sample LRLR: start 1 1 1 1 1; L at 0 -> c0=2; R at 1 -> c2=2; L at 2 ok (2>1); R at 3 -> c4=2. Result 2 1 2 1 2.

brief: Name s (<=100 letters), change at most k letters. Euphony = sum of bonuses c(x,y) over adjacent letter pairs. Maximize euphony.
key_idea: dp[i][j][c] = best euphony of the first i letters using j changes with letter i equal to c.
solution: 1) bonus[26][26] from input (default 0). 2) dp[0][ (c!=s0) ][c] = 0 for all c (if within k). 3) dp[i][j + (c!=s_i)][c] = max over prev letter q of dp[i-1][j][q] + bonus[q][c]. 4) Answer = max over j<=k, c of dp[n-1][j][c]. 5) Use -INF for unreachable.
dry_run: Sample winner, k=4 -> 'looser': lo(13)+oo(8)+os(8)+se(7) = 36.

brief: n targets with (x, y, appearance time t, hit probability p). The sight moves at speed 1 and starts anywhere. Maximize expected number of hits.
key_idea: Sort by time; dp[i] = p_i + max dp[j] over earlier targets reachable in time (distance <= t_i - t_j); like LIS on a DAG.
solution: 1) Sort targets by t. 2) dp[i] = p_i + max(0, max over j<i with (t_i - t_j)^2 >= (x_i-x_j)^2 + (y_i-y_j)^2 of dp[j]). 3) Use long long for squared comparisons. 4) Answer = max dp; print with 10 decimals.

brief: Two distinct words S, T of length n. Count words W of length n+1 such that deleting one character of W gives S and deleting one (possibly other) character gives T.
key_idea: Only the span [l, r] between the first and last differing positions matters; W is valid via S shifted by one inside it either way.
solution: 1) l = first index with S[l] != T[l], r = last such index. 2) Option A valid if S[l+1..r] == T[l..r-1] (W = S[0..l-1] + T[l] + S[l..]). 3) Option B valid if T[l+1..r] == S[l..r-1]. 4) Answer = A + B (they give different W since S != T).
dry_run: Sample reading/trading: l=0, r=1. A: S[1..1]='e' vs T[0..0]='t' no. B: T[1..1]='r' vs S[0..0]='r' yes -> 1 ('treading').

brief: Complete directed graph on n<=60 cities, m car types each with its own n x n time matrix. Queries (s,t,k): minimum travel time from s to t with at most k car changes.
key_idea: Floyd per car, take the per-pair minimum over cars as 'one segment', then min-plus multiply to allow more segments; more than n changes never help.
solution: 1) For each car run Floyd-Warshall. 2) one[i][j] = min over cars. 3) best[0] = one; best[c] = min(best[c-1], best[c-1] (x) one) via min-plus product, for c up to n. 4) Query: best[min(k, n)][s][t].
complexity: O(m n^3 + n^4) preprocessing, O(1) per query
dry_run: Sample: with 1 change (k=1) best path 1->4 takes 4; with 2 changes it drops to 3 (outputs 3,4,3).

brief: String s (<=1e5) and up to 10 boring strings (length <= 10). Find the longest substring of s containing no boring string; print its length and start.
key_idea: Sliding window: whenever a boring string ends at r, the window's left end must move past that occurrence's start.
solution: 1) left = 0, best = 0, pos = 0. 2) For r = 0..|s|-1: for each boring b ending at r (r-|b|+1 >= 0 and substring matches): left = max(left, r-|b|+2). 3) If r-left+1 > best: best = r-left+1, pos = left. 4) Print best and pos.
dry_run: Sample: window ending at index 15 starting after 's' of 'str' (index 4) gives 'traight_alon' of length 12 -> '12 4'.

brief: Binary stripe of length n (<=1000). A move picks two adjacent equal-colored squares and repaints them arbitrarily. Minimum moves to make the stripe alternate, or -1.
key_idea: A move can fix two adjacent wrong cells at once only in special cases; the answer equals the Hamming distance to the closer alternating pattern (verified by brute force), and it is always achievable.
solution: 1) d = number of positions where s differs from 0101... 2) Answer = min(d, n - d) (the other pattern 1010... differs in n-d positions). 3) Never -1.
dry_run: Sample 111010: vs 101010 differs at index 1 only -> d=1 (other pattern 5) -> 1.

brief: n cubes with colors; delete at most k cubes. Maximize the longest run of equal colors after deletion.
key_idea: For each color, take a window of its occurrences; cubes to delete = span length - count; two pointers keep that <= k.
solution: 1) pos[c] = list of indices of color c. 2) For each color: i=0; for j over its list: while (pos[j]-pos[i]+1) - (j-i+1) > k: i++. 3) ans = max(ans, j-i+1). 4) Print ans.
dry_run: Sample: color 1 at 0,2,3,6,7: window [2,3,6,7] span 6, count 4, deletions 2 <= k=2 -> 4.

brief: Paint n boards (heights h_i) red or green with total red area <= a and green area <= b. Minimize sum over adjacent different-colored boards of min(h_i, h_{i+1}); -1 if impossible. (Uses input.txt/output.txt.)
key_idea: dp[i][red area][color of board i] = min unattractiveness; green area is implied by prefix sum minus red area.
solution: 1) pre = prefix heights; dp[r][c] for current board (rolling). 2) Board 0: dp[h0][red]=0, dp[0][green]=0. 3) Board i: for each r, previous color pc, new color c: newR = r + (c==red ? h_i : 0); cost += (pc != c) ? min(h_{i-1}, h_i) : 0. 4) Answer = min over r <= a with pre[n] - r <= b of dp[r][*]; else -1. 5) Open input.txt/output.txt.
dry_run: Sample a=5,b=7, h=3 3 4 1 (total 11): e.g. red {4,1} (5), green {3,3} (6): one color boundary between boards 2 and 3 costs min(3,4)=3. Answer 3.

brief: Two bots each make exactly N moves in an optimal strategy; every move creates a new state. Count all states reachable while neither bot exceeds N moves, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: States are lattice paths (i,j) with i,j <= N moves; the number of distinct states is sum over cells of C(i+j, i) = C(2N+2, N+1) - 1.
solution: 1) Count = sum_{i=0}^{N} sum_{j=0}^{N} C(i+j, i) = C(2N+2, N+1) - 1 (hockey-stick identity twice). 2) Precompute factorials up to 2N+2 and modular inverses. 3) Print (C(2N+2,N+1) - 1) mod p.

brief: Permutation of n<=6; k<=4 times reverse a uniformly random segment [l,r] (l<=r). Expected number of inversions at the end.
key_idea: Tiny limits: enumerate all n(n+1)/2 segments at each of the k steps recursively (at most 21^4 leaves), averaging inversion counts.
solution: 1) S = n(n+1)/2 segments. 2) rec(p, k): if k==0 return inversions(p). Else average over all (l,r) of rec(reverse(p,l,r), k-1). 3) Print with 15 decimals. (G2/G3 need a pairwise-probability DP instead.)
dry_run: Sample 1 2 3, k=1: 6 segments; reversing [1,2] or [2,3] gives 1 inversion, [1,3] gives 3, single cells 0 -> (1+1+3)/6 = 0.8333.

brief: n board types a x b (rotatable unless square). Count sequences forming a fence of total length l where consecutive boards differ in type and each board's length equals the previous board's width; mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[len][type][orientation] = number of fences of total length len ending with that board placed that way; extend with a different type whose length equals the current width.
solution: 1) Orientation o gives (length, width) = (a,b) or (b,a); squares only one orientation. 2) dp[len_i][i][o] = 1 for every first board with length <= l. 3) For len ascending, for each (i,o) with count, for each j != i and orientation o2 with length(j,o2) == width(i,o) and len + length <= l: add. 4) Answer = sum of dp[l][*][*].
dry_run: Sample l=3, boards 1x2, 2x3: fences: [1x2 as length 1, width 2] + [2x3 length 2] = 3 ✓; [2x3 rotated: length 3] alone = 3 ✓. Answer 2.

brief: Given n (up to 100000 digits), output the smallest super lucky number (digits 4/7 only, equal counts) that is >= n.
key_idea: Match n's digits greedily with 4/7 while tight; at the first impossible digit, backtrack to the latest '4' that can become '7', then fill the rest minimally (4s then 7s).
solution: 1) If length L is odd: answer = (L+1)/2 fours then (L+1)/2 sevens. 2) Else build res tight: at position i with remaining counts c4,c7: d<4 -> place minimal fill (4 if c4 else 7) then fill rest minimally, done; d==4 and c4 -> 4, continue; 4<d<7 -> if c7: 7 + minimal fill, done; d==7 and c7 -> 7, continue; else fail at i. 3) If d==4 but c4==0 -> d<7 case: place 7 + fill. 4) On fail: scan j from i-1 down: if res[j]=='4' and sevens used before j < L/2: put 7 at j and fill minimally; done. 5) If no such j: answer has length L+2: (L/2+1) fours then sevens.
dry_run: Sample 4500: i0 '4' -> 4; i1 '5' (between 4 and 7) -> 7, then fill with remaining one 4 and one 7 -> 4747.

brief: 36-card deck (ranks 6..A, 4 suits), 18 cards each. Alternating turns: a 9 can always be played; lower cards need the next higher rank of the suit on the table, higher cards need the next lower. Must play if possible, else pass. First to empty their hand wins. Who wins with optimal play?
key_idea: On-table cards of each suit always form a contiguous rank interval containing 9, so a state is 4 intervals (25 options each) plus whose turn: memoized minimax over 25^4*2 states.
solution: 1) Rank index 0..8 (9 is index 3); per suit state: empty or [l,h] with l<=3<=h. 2) Legal card (r,s) for player: owned by player, not on table, and (suit empty and r==3) or r==l-1 or r==h+1. 3) win(state, turn): if no legal move -> !win(state, other) (pass). Else for each move: if the mover's on-table count becomes 18 -> win; else if !win(next, other) -> win. 4) Memoize; print Alice if win(empty, Alice).
dry_run: Own example: the search starts from the empty table; Alice must play one of her 9s first (only legal cards). For sample 1 the memoized search returns win -> 'Alice'.

brief: Bracket string (length up to 1e6). Output the length of the longest regular bracket substring and how many substrings have that length ('0 1' if none).
key_idea: Stack of indices with a sentinel: on ')' pop; if the stack becomes empty push i as new base, else the valid run ending at i has length i - top.
solution: 1) stack = [-1]. 2) '(' -> push i. 3) ')' -> pop; if empty push i; else len = i - top: if len > best: best=len, cnt=1; else if len == best: cnt++. 4) If best == 0 print '0 1' else best cnt.
dry_run: Sample )((())))(()()): run '((()))' at 1..6 gives 6 (cnt 1); later '(()())' at 8..13 gives 6 (cnt 2). Output 6 2.

brief: Line of n<=500 colored gems; each second remove one contiguous palindromic substring. Minimum seconds to remove everything.
key_idea: dp[l][r]: either remove c[l] alone, or pair c[l] with an equal c[k] so it disappears together with the last palindrome of the inner part dp[l+1][k-1].
solution: 1) dp[l][r] for l>r is 0; dp[i][i]=1. 2) dp[l][r] = 1 + dp[l+1][r]. 3) If c[l]==c[l+1]: dp[l][r] = min(.., 1 + dp[l+2][r]). 4) For k in l+2..r with c[l]==c[k]: dp[l][r] = min(.., dp[l+1][k-1] + dp[k+1][r]). 5) Answer dp[0][n-1].

brief: n<=1e6 numbers and m<=1000. Is there a non-empty subsequence whose sum is divisible by m?
key_idea: If n >= m, pigeonhole on prefix sums mod m guarantees YES; otherwise n < m and a reachable-remainder DP costs O(m^2).
solution: 1) If n >= m print YES. 2) Else can[r] = some non-empty subset has sum = r mod m. 3) For each a: new = copy; new[a%m]=true; for r with can[r]: new[(r+a)%m]=true. 4) YES iff can[0].

brief: T queries [L, R] (up to 1e18): count integers with at most 3 nonzero decimal digits.
key_idea: count(X) of classy numbers in [0, X] by walking digits of X: when placing a smaller digit at a position, the remaining L positions are free with at most (3 - used) nonzeros: sum_j C(L,j) 9^j.
solution: 1) free(L, k) = sum_{j=0}^{k} C(L,j)*9^j (k<0 -> 0). 2) count(X): used=0; for each digit d of X with L digits after it: if d>0: add free(L, 3-used) (put 0 here) + (d-1)*free(L, 3-used-1) (put 1..d-1); then used++ ; if used>3 stop. 3) If walk finished with used<=3 add 1 (X itself). 4) Answer = count(R) - count(L-1).

brief: n heights; for each group size x = 1..n, output the maximum over contiguous segments of length x of the segment minimum.
key_idea: Each a_i is the minimum of a maximal window of length len_i (between previous and next smaller); ans[len_i] = max(a_i), then ans[x] = max(ans[x], ans[x+1]).
solution: 1) Monotonic stack: L[i] = index of previous strictly smaller (or -1), R[i] = next smaller-or-equal (or n). 2) len = R[i]-L[i]-1; best[len] = max(best[len], a_i). 3) For x = n-1 down to 1: best[x] = max(best[x], best[x+1]). 4) Print best[1..n].
dry_run: Sample: 6 is min of window length 1 -> best[1]=6; 4 (at index 3 or 5) spans 3 -> best[3]=4; 5 spans 1. After suffix max: 6 4 4 3 3 2 2 1 1 1.

brief: Tree with vertex values a_v. For a root v, cost = sum of dist(i, v) * a_i. Maximize over all roots.
key_idea: Rerooting: moving the root from parent p to child c changes cost by S - 2*sub[c] (S = total of a, sub = subtree sum of c).
solution: 1) Root at 1: compute sub[v] (subtree sums) and cost(1) = sum depth*a. 2) In BFS order: cost[c] = cost[p] + S - 2*sub[c]. 3) Answer = max cost. 4) long long, iterative traversal.
dry_run: Sample: computing cost at every vertex via the shift formula, the maximum is 121 (attained at vertex 3).

brief: Fence of n planks with heights a_i; a 1-wide brush paints vertical strokes (one plank) or horizontal strokes (contiguous at a fixed height). Minimum strokes to paint everything.
key_idea: Divide and conquer: for a segment, either paint every plank vertically (length strokes) or paint horizontally up to its minimum, then recurse on the pieces above.
solution: 1) solve(l, r, base): if l > r return 0. 2) m = min(a[l..r]); cost = m - base. 3) Split [l,r] at positions with a == m; cost += solve(piece, m) for each piece. 4) Return min(r-l+1, cost). 5) Answer solve(0, n-1, 0).
dry_run: Sample 2 2 1 2 1: min 1 -> 1 stroke; pieces [2,2] (base 1) -> min(2, 1+0)=1, [2] -> 1. Total 1+1+1 = 3 (< 5 vertical).

brief: Array of distinct integers (values <= 1e6). Operation: append gcd(a_i, a_j) if it's not already present. Maximum number of operations.
key_idea: A value g can eventually be produced iff it's absent and the gcd of all present multiples of g equals g; count such g.
solution: 1) present[v] for v <= 1e6. 2) For g = 1..MAX: if present[g] skip. 3) G = 0; for multiples m = g, 2g, ...: if present[m] G = gcd(G, m); stop early if G == g. 4) If G == g count++. 5) Print count.

brief: n coins (values <= 500), pay exactly k with a subset; list all x that can be formed as a sub-sum of some subset summing to k.
key_idea: 2D knapsack: dp[s] = bitset of sub-sums x achievable inside some subset with sum s; adding coin c: dp[s+c] |= dp[s] | (dp[s] << c).
solution: 1) dp[0] = {0}. 2) For each coin c, for s = k-c down to 0: dp[s+c] |= dp[s] | (dp[s] << c). 3) Output all x with dp[k][x] set, count first.
complexity: O(n * k * k / 64) time, O(k^2) bits
dry_run: Sample k=18 coins 5 6 1 10 12 2: subsets {5,1,12}, {6,10,2}, {5,1,10,2}... union of their sub-sums gives 16 values 0 1 2 3 5 6 7 8 10 11 12 13 15 16 17 18.

brief: Rooted Dead Bush of level n is built recursively; choose vertex-disjoint claws (center + 3 child leaves) to color yellow. Max yellow vertices for level n (<= 2e6), mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: A level-n RDB is a root whose children are one level-(n-1) and two level-(n-2) RDBs; take their answers, and the root's claw can be added exactly when n % 3 == 0.
solution: 1) dp[1]=dp[2]=0. 2) dp[n] = dp[n-1] + 2*dp[n-2] + (n%3==0 ? 4 : 0) mod p. 3) Precompute up to 2e6, answer queries.
complexity: O(max n) precomputation, O(1) per query

brief: Choose X to minimize max_i (a_i XOR X); print that minimum (a_i < 2^30).
key_idea: Recurse on bits from the top: if all numbers share the current bit, X can cancel it; otherwise that bit is forced into the answer and X picks the cheaper half.
solution: 1) solve(v, b): if v empty or b<0 return 0. 2) Split v into zeros/ones by bit b. 3) If one side empty: return solve(other side, b-1). 4) Else return (1<<b) + min(solve(zeros,b-1), solve(ones,b-1)). 5) Answer solve(all, 29).
dry_run: Sample 1 2 3: bit1 splits {1} and {2,3}: 2 + min(solve({1}), solve({2,3})): bit0 of {1} -> 0; so answer 2.

brief: Tree tag: Alice at a (jump <= da), Bob at b (jump <= db), Alice moves first; Alice wins if she ever lands on Bob. Who wins?
key_idea: Alice wins iff dist(a,b) <= da, or the tree diameter <= 2*da (she controls the center), or db <= 2*da (Bob can never jump past her).
solution: 1) BFS from a to get dist(a,b). 2) Diameter via double BFS. 3) If dist <= da or 2*da >= diameter or db <= 2*da -> Alice, else Bob.
dry_run: Sample1: star centered at 1, a=3,b=2, da=1, db=2: dist 2 > 1, diameter 2 <= 2*da=2 -> Alice.

brief: Row of colored squares; pick a starting square, then each turn recolor its connected same-color block. Minimum turns to make the row one color.
key_idea: Compress equal neighbors; dp[l][r] = turns to make block l..r one color, growing from inside; if the ends match, one turn merges both.
solution: 1) Compress runs into array c of length m. 2) dp[i][i] = 0. 3) dp[l][r] = (c[l]==c[r]) ? dp[l+1][r-1] + 1 : min(dp[l+1][r], dp[l][r-1]) + 1. 4) Answer dp[0][m-1].

brief: Array a (n<=2000, values<=1e9). Find the longest subsequence whose LCM is not in a (empty subsequence has LCM 0).
key_idea: If some a_i doesn't divide max(a), the LCM of everything exceeds max and is absent -> n. Otherwise every LCM is a divisor of max: try each divisor d not in a, take all a_i dividing d, and check their LCM equals d.
solution: 1) mx = max a. If any a_i does not divide mx -> print n. 2) Enumerate divisors d of mx (O(sqrt mx)). 3) For each d not in the set of a: cnt = 0, L = 1; for each a_i dividing d: cnt++, L = lcm(L, a_i). If L == d: ans = max(ans, cnt). 4) Print ans (0 if none).
dry_run: Sample 1 2 4 8 16: all divide 16; divisors 1,2,4,8,16 are all present -> answer 0.

brief: Array a and integer x (|x|<=100). Optionally multiply one contiguous subarray by x; maximize the maximum subarray sum (empty allowed).
key_idea: Kadane with 3 phases: before the multiplied segment, inside it, after it.
solution: 1) d0,d1,d2 = best sum of a subarray ending at i in phase 0/1/2 (fresh start allowed). 2) n0 = max(d0,0) + a; n1 = max(d0,d1,0) + a*x; n2 = max(d1,d2,0) + a. 3) ans = max(ans, n0, n1, n2), starting ans = 0. 4) long long (|a*x| <= 1e11).
dry_run: Sample x=-2, a=-3 8 -2 1 -6: take 8 normally then multiply [-2,1,-6] -> 8+4-2+12 = 22.

brief: Remove the minimum number of elements so that for every pair, one divides the other.
key_idea: A beautiful array sorted is a divisor chain; dp[v] = longest chain ending at value v, pushed forward to multiples (harmonic sum).
solution: 1) cnt[v] for v <= 2e5. 2) For v ascending: dp[v] += cnt[v] (dp starts as best from divisors, 0 initially); then for multiples m = 2v, 3v, ...: dp[m] = max(dp[m], dp[v]). 3) best = max dp; answer = n - best.
dry_run: Sample 7 9 3 14 63: chain 3 -> 9 -> 63 (or 7 -> 63) gives 3 elements; remove 5-3 = 2.

brief: Binary string of lamps and k. Flip the minimum number of lamps so that consecutive lit lamps are exactly k apart (0 or 1 lit lamps is fine).
key_idea: Lit lamps must be a contiguous run within one residue class mod k; cost = total ones + sum over chosen of (s==0 ? +1 : -1), minimized by a min-subarray (Kadane) per residue.
solution: 1) T = total ones. 2) For each residue r in 0..k-1: walk positions r, r+k, ...; value v = (s[p]=='1') ? -1 : +1; Kadane for minimum subarray sum (allow empty = 0). 3) Answer = T + min over residues of that minimum.
dry_run: Sample '010001010', k=2: T=3. Residue 1 (positions 1,3,5,7 = 1,0,0,1)... best is to keep the lamps at 5 and 7 (residue 1: values for 5,7 = -1,-1) -> T-2 = 1, turning off lamp 1. Answer 1.

brief: Cards with prices a_i (none equal x). Split into the minimum number of contiguous segments so that no segment has a subset with product exactly x.
key_idea: Greedily extend each segment as long as possible; track which divisors of x are achievable as subset products inside the current segment.
solution: 1) ans = 1, set S = {1} of achievable divisor products in current segment. 2) For each a: if x % a != 0 skip (can never help). 3) New products = {d*a : d in S, x % (d*a) == 0}. If x is among them: start a new segment: ans++, S = {1, a}. Else S |= new products. 4) Print ans. Use a bool array over divisors of x (<=128).
dry_run: Sample x=4, a=2 3 6 2 1 2: seg1 [2,3,6] (products 2,1...; next 2 would make 4) -> new seg [2,1] then next 2 makes 4 -> new seg [2]. Total 3.

brief: Stack of n mobs with healths h_i (mob 1 at bottom). Each attack deals 1 damage to any mob; when a mob dies, mobs above fall and the new bottom takes fall damage equal to the number of mobs it was standing on (cascading). Minimum attacks to kill all.
key_idea: Each mob i either gets 1 fall damage (mob i-1 dies under it as a stack bottom) or gets i-1 fall damage by killing mob i-1 first while everything below is intact.
solution: 1) dp[0]=0, dp[1]=h_1. 2) dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + h_i - 1, dp[i-2] + h_{i-1} + max(0, h_i - (i-1))). 3) Answer dp[n]. 4) long long. (Verified against brute force on small stacks.)

brief: n plots with height limits m_i (n<=5e5). Choose heights 1<=a_i<=m_i forming a single peak (non-decreasing then non-increasing) with maximum total; print the heights.
key_idea: L[i] = best total of a non-decreasing prefix ending with a_i = m_i, computed with a monotonic stack (previous smaller element); same for suffix; pick the best peak.
solution: 1) Stack of indices with increasing m: for i, pop while m[top] >= m[i]; j = top or -1; L[i] = (j>=0 ? L[j] : 0) + m[i]*(i-j). 2) Symmetric R[i] from the right. 3) Peak p = argmax L[i] + R[i] - m[i]. 4) Build: a[p]=m[p]; go left a[i] = min(m[i], a[i+1]); go right a[i] = min(m[i], a[i-1]). 5) long long.
dry_run: Sample 1 2 3 2 1: peak at index 2 with L=6, R=6 -> total 9: heights 1 2 3 2 1.

brief: Islands 0..30000 with gems. Start at 0, first jump d, each next jump is l-1, l or l+1 of the previous (positive). Maximize gems collected on landed islands.
key_idea: Jump length can deviate from d by at most ~245 (1+2+...+245 > 30000), so dp[position][length - d + 250] fits in memory.
solution: 1) gem[p] counts. 2) dp[p][o] = max gems arriving at p with last jump length d + o - 250; -1 = unreachable. dp[d][250] = gem[0] + gem[d]. 3) For p ascending, each reachable (p,o): for dl in -1..1: L = len + dl; if L >= 1 and p+L <= 30000: dp[p+L][o+dl] = max(.., dp[p][o] + gem[p+L]). 4) Answer = max over all dp.
dry_run: Sample d=10, gems at 10,21,27,27: 0 -> 10 (1 gem) -> 19 (jump 9) -> 27 (jump 8): 3 gems.

brief: Color each element of a white/black; seg(x) = number of runs after merging equal neighbors. Maximize seg(white subsequence) + seg(black subsequence).
key_idea: Keep the last values x, y of the two subsequences; if a matches one of them put it on the other; if it matches neither, replace the one whose value reappears sooner.
solution: 1) nxt[i] = next index with the same value (INF if none); keep last indices/values of both sequences. 2) If a_i differs from both: append to the sequence whose last value's next occurrence is nearer (so that value no longer blocks); ans++. 3) If a_i equals exactly one last value: append to the other; ans++. 4) If equal to both: append anywhere, no gain. 5) Print ans.
dry_run: Sample 1 1 2 2 3 3 3: alternate copies: white 1 2 3, black 1 2 3 3 -> 3 + 3 = 6.

brief: k (<=5) permutations of 1..n (n<=1000). Length of their longest common subsequence.
key_idea: Value u can precede v in the LCS iff u comes before v in every permutation; longest path in this DAG, processed in the order of the first permutation.
solution: 1) pos[j][v] = index of v in permutation j. 2) Process values in the order of permutation 1: dp[v] = 1 + max dp[u] for earlier u with pos[j][u] < pos[j][v] for all j. 3) Answer = max dp.
complexity: O(n^2 * k) time, O(n k) space
dry_run: Sample: perms 1423, 4123, 1243. Order 1,4,2,3: dp1=1, dp4=1 (4 before 1 in perm2), dp2=2 (after 1 everywhere), dp3=3 (after 1,2). Answer 3.

brief: Tree with values a_i < 2^20. Spell: XOR c into the whole subtree of v at cost size*c. For every root r, minimum cost to make all values equal.
key_idea: For a fixed root, each edge (parent p, child c) must be fixed exactly once with c = a_p XOR a_c on the child's subtree: cost = sum (a_p^a_c) * size(child side); reroot by swapping the side size.
solution: 1) Root at 1: subtree sizes sz; ans[1] = sum over edges (a_p ^ a_c) * sz[c]. 2) Reroot: for child c of p with w = a_p ^ a_c: ans[c] = ans[p] + w * (n - 2*sz[c]). 3) BFS order, iterative. 4) long long; print all.

brief: n rectangles a_i x b_i; coloring one cell is one operation; each fully colored row or column of a rectangle gives 1 point. Minimum operations to get at least k points (k<=100), or -1.
key_idea: Within one rectangle, fully coloring r rows and q columns costs r*a + q*b - r*q cells for r+q points; take the min per point count, then a min-cost knapsack over rectangles.
solution: 1) For each rectangle compute c[p] = min over r+q=p (0<=r<=b rows, 0<=q<=a columns) of r*a + q*b - r*q, for p <= min(k, a+b) (note a 1x1 cell gives 2 points for 1 operation). 2) dp[j] = min operations for j points (cap j at k), dp[0]=0. 3) For each rectangle: nd[min(k, j+p)] = min(dp[j] + c[p]). 4) Answer dp[k] or -1.
dry_run: Sample1: 6x3, k=4: each step paints a column of 3 cells (min(6,3)=3): 4 points = 12 operations.

brief: n weapon classes (forge costs a_i ingots, melting returns b_i < a_i), m metal stocks c_j. Each forge and each melt gives 1 experience. Maximize experience.
key_idea: Always forge+melt the weapon with the smallest net loss a_i - b_i among those affordable; precompute best[x] and dp[x] for x <= 1e6, and jump large stocks down in one step.
solution: 1) A = max a (<= 1e6). best[x] = min (a_i - b_i) over a_i <= x (prefix min over a). 2) dp[x] = (best[x] < INF) ? 2 + dp[x - best[x]] : 0 for x = 1..A. 3) For each c_j: if c_j > A: k = ceil((c_j - A)/best[A]); exp += 2k; c_j -= k*best[A]. Then exp += dp[c_j]. 4) Sum over metals (long long).
dry_run: Sample: total 12 experience over metals 10, 4, 7 (e.g. class 1 with loss 1 used repeatedly on metal 10).

brief: Sequence of n distinct values (1..n). Count increasing subsequences of length exactly k+1 (k <= 10).
key_idea: dp[len][v] = number of increasing subsequences of length len ending with value v; Fenwick trees (one per length) give prefix sums over smaller values.
solution: 1) k+1 Fenwick trees over values 1..n. 2) For each a: for len = k+1 down to 2: c = bit[len-1].query(a-1); bit[len].add(a, c). Then bit[1].add(a, 1). 3) Answer = bit[k+1].query(n). 4) Use unsigned long long / long long (answer <= 8e18).
complexity: O(n k log n) time, O(n k) space

brief: Players alternately append letters keeping the word a prefix of one of n strings; the player unable to move loses. k games are played, loser of a game starts the next; winner of the last game wins. Does the first player win?
key_idea: On the trie compute canWin and canLose for the player to move at the root; if the first player can control both outcomes he wins; if he can only win, the result alternates with k's parity.
solution: 1) Build a trie of all strings. 2) Post-order: leaf: win=false, lose=true. Internal: win = any child with !win; lose = any child with !lose. 3) If win && lose -> First. 4) If win && !lose -> First iff k is odd. 5) If !win -> Second.
dry_run: Sample {a,b}, k=3: root has leaf children -> win=true, lose=false -> k odd -> First.

brief: n locks with capacities v_i; open pipes add 1 liter/s into a lock, overflow goes to the next lock. For each query t, minimum pipes so that all locks are full after t seconds, or -1.
key_idea: Best is to open the first p pipes; the first i locks can receive at most i liters/s, so minimal possible time is max_i ceil(S_i / i); with t allowed the needed pipes are ceil(S_n / t).
solution: 1) Prefix sums S_i. 2) Tmin = max over i of ceil(S_i / i). 3) For query t: if t < Tmin print -1. 4) Else print ceil(S_n / t) (opening the first p pipes; each earlier lock fills in time because t >= Tmin).
